- **Security-relevant, found during the PostgreSQL provider migration: harden `SensitiveDataAccessLog`'s tamper protection with Row-Level Security.** `REVOKE UPDATE, DELETE ON sensitive_data_access_logs FROM PUBLIC` (the literal ADR-0005 instruction, now built) was verified — against current PostgreSQL documentation, not assumed from the SQL Server `DENY` mental model — to be structurally weaker than the SQL Server original it replaced: PostgreSQL's privilege model has no override concept, so a role explicitly `GRANT`ed `UPDATE`/`DELETE` directly (not via `PUBLIC`), or that owns the table, is completely unaffected by this `REVOKE` — see `docs/adr/0004-sensitive-data-access-control.md` §4 pass 6 and `openwiki/access-control.md`'s "Tamper protection" section for the full, cited explanation. The real DENY-equivalent — `ALTER TABLE ... FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` plus `CREATE POLICY ... FOR UPDATE USING (false)` / `FOR DELETE USING (false)`, which blocks even the table owner, only a superuser/`BYPASSRLS` role exempt — was deliberately not built in the provider-migration item itself: it requires an explicit permissive policy for every command that must keep working (`SELECT`/`INSERT`) or that command is default-denied too the moment row security is enabled, and a mistake there risks silently breaking the audit interceptor's own `INSERT` path (the single most safety-critical write in this codebase) — too much new risk for what was scoped as a same-provider port, not a redesign. Higher scrutiny warranted than most items in this queue given what's at stake; read the migration's own doc comment (`RevokeUpdateDeleteOnSensitiveDataAccessLog.cs`) and the ADR/openwiki sections above before starting, and prove the `SELECT`/`INSERT` permissive policies actually work (not just that `UPDATE`/`DELETE` are blocked) with a real, not tautological, test.
